lead.en: Giants with the biggest eggs vanish as people burn the forests

summary.en: Elephant birds, flightless giants up to 3 m tall that laid the largest eggs ever known, vanished between about 800 and 1050 according to the latest radiocarbon dates, along with Madagascar's hippos. Human burning of forest for pasture is blamed.

title.en: Stephen I, first king of Hungary

lead.en: The Magyar nomads become a Christian kingdom

summary.en: Around 1000, Stephen of the Árpád dynasty was crowned with a crown sent by the Pope. He converted the country, founded bishoprics and turned the Magyar tribal union into a European kingdom.

lead.en: Star-guided canoes find islands in the middle of the Pacific

summary.en: Polynesian navigators in double-hulled canoes, steering by stars, swells and birds, reached the Hawaiian Islands. The date is debated; modern radiocarbon studies point to roughly 1000–1200.

lead.en: The shrine from which, by tradition, voyagers set out

summary.en: On Raiatea in the Society Islands, by various estimates around 1000, a marae complex arose: paved courts with upright stones for ceremonies. Taputapuātea became a shared sanctuary of East Polynesia: by tradition chiefs sailed here from other archipelagos, and stones taken from it were set into the foundations of new marae on distant islands. It has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2017.

lead.en: A lady-in-waiting writes lists of 'hateful things'

summary.en: A lady-in-waiting to Empress Teishi jotted down observations, gossip and opinions on everything. Its best-known parts are 164 lists such as 'Hateful Things' and 'Things That Make the Heart Beat Faster' — a Japanese classic that reads like a blog.

title.en: A Byzantine bride’s fork in Venice

lead.en: Venice is scandalised by a Greek noblewoman eating with a fork

summary.en: Maria Argyropoulina, niece of the Byzantine emperor, married the son of the Doge of Venice and ate with a golden fork. The theologian Peter Damian condemned such luxury, and her early death was called divine punishment.

lead.en: A star brighter than Venus, bright enough to read by

summary.en: In spring 1006 the brightest stellar event in recorded history flared in the constellation Lupus, brighter than Venus, bright enough to read by at night. It was described by the astronomer Ali ibn Ridwan in Cairo and by Chinese, Japanese and European chroniclers.

lead.en: Murasaki Shikibu writes what may be the world's first novel

summary.en: The court lady Murasaki Shikibu wrote the story of Prince Genji's loves and life at the imperial court. Often called the world's first novel, it is the summit of classical Japanese prose.

lead.en: A 66-metre granite tower, emblem of Chola power

summary.en: King Rajaraja I of the Chola dynasty completed a vast Shiva temple in his capital. Its granite vimana, about 66 metres high, was among the tallest structures of its time, and its walls are covered with inscriptions on gifts and temple staff. With two other Chola temples, it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

lead.en: 50,000 couplets: the national epic of Iran

summary.en: The poet Ferdowsi spent over 30 years on the Book of Kings, some 50,000 couplets about Iran's kings and heroes from the creation to the Arab conquest. He deliberately avoided Arabic words, and the poem helped preserve the Persian language. The Shahnameh is regarded as Iran's national epic; the poet finished its final version in 1010.

title.en: Thăng Long, the future Hanoi, becomes the capital

lead.en: Emperor Lý moves his capital to the Red River

summary.en: Lý Thái Tổ, founder of the Lý dynasty, decreed the move of the capital from mountain-girt Hoa Lư to Đại La on the Red River and named the city Thăng Long, 'Ascending Dragon'. It remained Vietnam's capital for almost eight centuries and is today Hanoi, which celebrated its millennium in 2010.

lead.en: An English monk leaps from a tower on home-made wings

summary.en: According to William of Malmesbury, Eilmer strapped wings to his hands and feet, jumped from the abbey tower and flew more than a furlong — about 200 metres — before crashing, breaking both legs and limping ever after. He blamed it on forgetting to fit a tail.

title.en: Ibn al-Haytham writes the Book of Optics

lead.en: A landmark work on light, written under house arrest

summary.en: Ordered by Caliph al-Hakim to tame the Nile floods, the scholar realised it was impossible and, legend says, feigned madness to escape the ruler's wrath. Under house arrest he showed that we see because light enters the eye, not because rays leave it.

lead.en: Basil II blinds thousands of Bulgarian captives

summary.en: Byzantine Emperor Basil II crushed the army of the First Bulgarian Empire. Chroniclers say he blinded thousands of captives, leaving every hundredth man one eye to lead the rest home; Tsar Samuel died at the sight. Bulgaria soon became part of Byzantium, and Basil was called the Bulgar-Slayer.

lead.en: Vladimir's sons die in a feud and become the first saints of Rus'

summary.en: After Vladimir the Great died in 1015, his sons Boris and Gleb were killed in the struggle for Kiev; the chronicle blames their brother Sviatopolk, called the Accursed. In 1019 Yaroslav the Wise drove Sviatopolk out, and Boris and Gleb became the first saints of Rus', revered as passion-bearers.

title.en: Russkaya Pravda of Yaroslav the Wise

lead.en: Fines replace blood feuds in Rus' first written law code

summary.en: The oldest part of Rus' law, the 'Pravda of Yaroslav', is traditionally linked to Yaroslav the Wise and dated to around 1016. Russkaya Pravda restricted blood feud and introduced a system of monetary fines.

lead.en: Vikings reach America nearly 500 years before Columbus

summary.en: Around 1000, Norse seafarers led by Leif Erikson reached North America, which they called Vinland. Tree-ring analysis of wood from L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland proves Norse presence there in 1021, nearly 500 years before Columbus.

lead.en: Merchant IOUs become the empire's own currency

summary.en: The Song government began official issue of jiaozi in Sichuan, the world's first state paper money. Earlier, merchants of Chengdu had issued such notes to avoid carrying heavy iron coins.

lead.en: Mstislav beats Yaroslav; the brothers split Rus' on the Dnieper

summary.en: Mstislav of Tmutarakan defeated Yaroslav the Wise and his Varangian retinue. Under the peace of 1026 the brothers divided Rus' along the Dnieper: Mstislav took the left bank with Chernihiv, Yaroslav the right bank with Kiev. After Mstislav died in 1036, Yaroslav ruled alone.

lead.en: The textbook European doctors used for six centuries

summary.en: Ibn Sina (Avicenna) completed his five-volume Canon in 1025 while moving between the courts of Persian rulers. He combined Hippocrates, Galen and the experience of Islamic physicians, described contagion and set rules for testing drugs. Translated into Latin in the 12th century, it was taught in European universities until the 17th century.

lead.en: An Indian fleet weakens a maritime empire on Sumatra

summary.en: The fleet of the South Indian Chola empire under Rajendra I raided the cities of the maritime empire of Srivijaya on Sumatra and the Malay Peninsula. The raid weakened Srivijaya and showed the reach of Indian power in Southeast Asia.

lead.en: Yaroslav builds Rus' chief church on the model of Constantinople

summary.en: Yaroslav the Wise founded the Cathedral of Saint Sophia, the chief church of Rus', named after Hagia Sophia in Constantinople. Inside survive 11th-century mosaics and frescoes, including a portrait of Yaroslav's family and graffiti that tell historians about daily life.

title.en: First gunpowder formulas in the Wujing Zongyao

lead.en: China writes down the formula that will transform warfare

summary.en: China completed the military compendium Wujing Zongyao, containing the earliest known gunpowder formulas. It described incendiary and smoke bombs; gunpowder later spread to the Islamic world and Europe, transforming warfare.

lead.en: Pagan joins the Irrawaddy valley under Theravada Buddhism

summary.en: King Anawrahta turned the Pagan Kingdom into the first state to unite the Irrawaddy valley and established Theravada Buddhism there. His successors built thousands of pagodas and temples at Bagan.

lead.en: A Mississippi city grows to 10,000–20,000 people

summary.en: Around 1050, Cahokia in the Mississippi valley grew into the largest city in North America north of Mexico, with an estimated 10,000–20,000 people. At its heart stood Monks Mound, the largest earthen platform mound on the continent.

lead.en: Novgorodians write each other notes on birch bark

summary.en: From the 11th century, Novgorodians scratched letters on birch bark: IOUs, quarrels, a boy named Onfim's school exercises with drawings. Waterlogged soil has preserved over a thousand of them. Found since 1951, they showed literacy in Rus' was widespread, not confined to monasteries.

lead.en: Mutual excommunications split Christianity in two

summary.en: The papal legate Cardinal Humbert laid a bull excommunicating Patriarch Michael Cerularius on the altar of Hagia Sophia, and the patriarch anathematised the legates in turn. The schism split Christianity into Catholic and Orthodox churches.

lead.en: Seen in daylight for 23 days, it leaves behind the Crab Nebula

summary.en: On 4 July 1054 Song dynasty astronomers noted a 'guest star' that stayed visible in daylight for 23 days. Its remnant is the Crab Nebula. In the same year the Christian Church split into East and West.

lead.en: The oldest precisely dated East Slavic book

summary.en: Deacon Grigory copied the Gospels for Ostromir, the governor of Novgorod, and dated his work 1056–1057. The parchment book with vivid miniatures is kept in the National Library of Russia in St Petersburg.

lead.en: The Normans remake England's elite and its language

summary.en: Duke William of Normandy defeated the Anglo-Saxon king Harold II, who was killed in the battle. The Norman Conquest replaced the English elite, transformed the English language and bound England closely to continental Europe.

lead.en: An omen for King Harold, stitched into the Bayeux Tapestry

summary.en: In spring 1066 Halley's Comet hung over England and was taken as a bad omen for King Harold II. That autumn he died at Hastings, and the comet was stitched into the Bayeux Tapestry beside words saying people marvel at the star.

lead.en: An Andalusian geographer portrays a realm of gold and salt

summary.en: The Andalusian geographer al-Bakri described the capital of Ghana as a twin town with a Muslim merchant quarter and a royal residence. The Ghana Empire grew rich by controlling the trans-Saharan trade in gold and salt.

title.en: Battle of the Alta River and the Kiev uprising

lead.en: The Cumans rout Yaroslav's sons, and Kiev overthrows its prince

summary.en: The Cumans defeated the army of Yaroslav the Wise's three sons, Iziaslav, Sviatoslav and Vsevolod. The Kiev assembly demanded weapons to fight again and, when refused, rose up: Iziaslav fled to Poland, and Vseslav of Polotsk was freed from prison and put on the throne.

lead.en: Warriors from the Sahara build the city that named Morocco

summary.en: Around 1070 (traditionally 1062) the Almoravids, Berbers from the Sahara preaching a strict Islam, laid out Marrakesh. Under Yusuf ibn Tashfin they took Morocco and Muslim Spain, defeating Castile at Sagrajas in 1086. Marrakesh became the capital of a vast empire, and in many languages its name became the name of the whole country: Morocco.

lead.en: A Byzantine defeat opens Anatolia to the Turks

summary.en: Seljuk sultan Alp Arslan routed the Byzantine army and captured Emperor Romanos IV Diogenes. Turkic settlers then poured into Anatolia, and Byzantium's appeals to the West for help paved the way for the Crusades.

lead.en: Southern Africa's first state and its golden rhinoceros

summary.en: Around 1075 the capital of southern Africa's first state rose on a hill where the Limpopo and Shashe rivers meet. Its rulers lived on the summit, apart from their subjects, while ivory and gold went out through Swahili ports to the Indian Ocean. In 1933 a rhinoceros of gold foil was found in a royal grave. After Mapungubwe declined, power shifted to Great Zimbabwe.

lead.en: An emperor waits three days in the snow for papal pardon

summary.en: Excommunicated Emperor Henry IV stood for three days at the gates of Canossa castle in January 1077, begging Pope Gregory VII to lift the ban. The episode became a symbol of the struggle between Church and crown.

lead.en: Students hire law teachers — and the university is born

summary.en: The University of Bologna traditionally dates its founding to 1088. It grew out of student guilds studying Roman law and is considered the oldest university in continuous operation.

lead.en: The first account of the compass — and its slightly wrong north

summary.en: In retirement the scholar-official Shen Kuo wrote down everything he knew, including the first description of the magnetic compass and the observation that the needle does not point exactly north — plus the story of the commoner Bi Sheng, who invented movable type of baked clay in the 1040s.

title.en: Battle of Levounion: the end of the Pechenegs

lead.en: Byzantium and the Cumans wipe out the Pecheneg horde in a day

summary.en: For two centuries the Pechenegs raided Rus' and Byzantium; in 1036 Yaroslav the Wise defeated them outside Kyiv. On 29 April 1091 Alexios I Komnenos and his Cuman allies all but annihilated their horde in Thrace, and the Pechenegs vanished as a people.

lead.en: A water clock with the first known chain drive

summary.en: The Song official Su Song built a tower in the capital where a water wheel turned an armillary sphere and a celestial globe. Power ran through an endless chain — the oldest known, like a bicycle's — and 133 figurines struck and displayed the hours.

lead.en: Oldest English-speaking university, older than the Aztec state

summary.en: There is evidence of teaching at Oxford by 1096, and it grew rapidly after 1167, when Henry II barred English students from Paris. It is the oldest university in the English-speaking world.

lead.en: Princes make peace but lock Rus' into hereditary fiefs

summary.en: On 19 October 1097 the princes of Rus' met at Liubech to end their feuds. They proclaimed that 'each shall keep his patrimony', entrenching the division of Rus' into hereditary principalities.

lead.en: The First Crusade ends with a new kingdom in the Levant

summary.en: Knights of the First Crusade, proclaimed by Pope Urban II in 1095, stormed Jerusalem and massacred its inhabitants. The Kingdom of Jerusalem was founded, and the Crusades shaped relations between Europe and the Middle East for two centuries.

lead.en: The Khmer raise the world's largest religious monument

summary.en: The Khmer king Suryavarman II began building Angkor Wat, a temple to Vishnu and probably his own mausoleum. It is the world's largest religious monument and a symbol of Khmer power, featured today on the flag of Cambodia.

lead.en: The prince under whom Rus' is united around Kiev one last time

summary.en: After a popular uprising in 1113, the people of Kiev invited Vladimir Monomakh to the throne. He issued a statute curbing usury and briefly restored the unity of Rus', which broke apart after the death of his son Mstislav.

lead.en: 'Whence came the Rus' land': the chief chronicle of Rus'

summary.en: Around 1113 the monk Nestor compiled earlier records into a chronicle opening with 'whence came the Rus' land'. It is our source for the calling of the Varangians, Olga's revenge and Vladimir's choice of faith. It survives in later copies, and many of its stories are more legend than fact.

lead.en: The Jurchens take the Song capital and two emperors captive

summary.en: The army of the Jurchen Jin empire took Kaifeng and carried north Emperor Qinzong, his father Huizong and thousands of courtiers. The Song lost all of northern China. A surviving prince founded the Southern Song with its capital at Hangzhou, and the border with the Jin ran along the Huai River.

lead.en: Novgorod expels its prince and the veche takes power

summary.en: In 1136 Novgorod expelled Prince Vsevolod and began choosing for itself whom to invite as prince. Real power passed to the veche assembly, the posadnik and the archbishop. The rich trading city, linked to the Hanseatic League, stayed a republic for more than three centuries, until Moscow annexed it in 1478.

lead.en: Kara Khitai crush the Seljuks, feeding the Prester John myth

summary.en: The Kara Khitai under Yelü Dashi, who had fled west from northern China, routed the army of the Seljuk sultan Sanjar. Transoxiana came under their rule. Rumours of a distant eastern king defeating the Muslims reached Europe and fed the legend of a Christian ruler, Prester John.

lead.en: The first crusader state falls, prompting the Second Crusade

summary.en: Imad al-Din Zengi, atabeg of Mosul, took Edessa after a month-long siege; it was the capital of the first state founded by the crusaders. The news shocked Europe, and Pope Eugene III called the Second Crusade. Led by the kings of France and Germany, it ended in failure before Damascus in 1148.

lead.en: A Berber movement builds an empire from the Atlantic to Libya

summary.en: The Almohad movement, founded by the preacher Ibn Tumart among the Berbers of the Atlas, took Marrakesh under Caliph Abd al-Mu'min and ended the Almoravids. Their empire stretched from the Atlantic to Tripoli and took in Muslim Spain; the philosopher Averroes served at the Almohad court. Defeat at Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212 began its break-up.

lead.en: Yuri Dolgoruky invites an ally to a future capital

summary.en: Under the year 1147 the Hypatian Chronicle records Prince Yuri Dolgoruky of Suzdal inviting his ally Sviatoslav Olgovich to meet him at Moskov. It is the first chronicle mention of the future capital of Russia.

title.en: Hildegard of Bingen invents a language

lead.en: A 12th-century nun creates an 'unknown language'

summary.en: Abbess, composer and healer, Hildegard compiled a glossary of over a thousand words in her Lingua ignota, 'unknown language', and devised a 23-letter alphabet for it. Why is unclear — perhaps for mystical purposes; the language has no known grammar.

lead.en: An arithmetic book named, legend says, for a daughter

summary.en: Legend says Bhaskara calculated the auspicious moment for his daughter Lilavati's wedding and timed it with a water clock. She peeked in, a pearl from her dress fell into the vessel and spoiled the clock, and the moment passed. To console her he named his book of problems after her.

lead.en: Rooks shaped as berserkers biting their shields

summary.en: These 12th-century walrus-ivory pieces, probably made in Norway, were found in 1831 on the Scottish Isle of Lewis. Many have comically anxious faces, and four of the rooks are berserkers biting the rims of their shields in battle fury.

lead.en: The 12th century's best world map — with south at the top

summary.en: The Arab geographer al-Idrisi spent some 15 years gathering information at the court of Roger II, the Norman king of Sicily, finishing an atlas of 70 maps a few weeks before the king died in 1154. North is at the bottom, south at the top.

lead.en: Nearly two centuries of work on a model of French Gothic

summary.en: The first stone of Notre-Dame de Paris was laid in 1163 under Bishop Maurice de Sully. Construction lasted nearly two centuries and was completed around 1345.

title.en: Church of the Intercession on the Nerl

lead.en: A white-stone church in a meadow, the emblem of Vladimir Rus'

summary.en: Andrey Bogolyubsky built the church where the Nerl meets the Klyazma, by tradition in memory of a son who died. Each spring the graceful white-stone church on its man-made mound stands amid the floodwaters. It is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

lead.en: The heart of Rus' shifts from the Dnieper to the northeast

summary.en: Andrey Bogolyubsky, prince of Vladimir-Suzdal, sent an army against Kiev, and the city was plundered. Yet Andrey did not move there; he installed a younger brother and stayed in Vladimir. It symbolised a shift: the 'mother of Rus' cities' was no longer the centre of Rus'.

lead.en: After two Shia centuries, Egypt returns to Sunni rule

summary.en: The Kurdish commander Saladin, vizier to the last Fatimid caliph al-Adid, had the Friday prayer said in the name of the Abbasid caliph after al-Adid's death. The Shia Fatimid Caliphate, which had ruled Egypt since 969, came to an end. Saladin founded the Ayyubid dynasty and united Egypt and Syria.

title.en: The Leaning Tower of Pisa is begun

lead.en: The bell tower started leaning at the second floor

summary.en: The cathedral bell tower was begun in 1173 on a foundation just three metres deep in soft soil. By 1178, at the second floor, it had begun to sink; wars halted the work for long stretches, and the tower was finished only in the 14th century — already leaning.

title.en: Nan Madol, the stone city on water

lead.en: A "Venice of the Pacific" stacked from basalt logs

summary.en: Off the coast of Pohnpei, nearly a hundred artificial islets are linked by a web of canals. Their walls are stacked log-cabin style from hexagonal basalt columns, some weighing several tons. By various estimates major construction began around 1180–1200, when this was the capital of the Saudeleur dynasty that ruled the whole island. How the columns were moved without metal or pulleys is still debated.

lead.en: A Buddhist king builds the Bayon's stone faces and 100 hospitals

summary.en: After the Cham sacked Angkor in 1177, Jayavarman VII drove them out and was crowned in 1181. He built the new capital of Angkor Thom with the Bayon temple and its giant stone faces, as well as over a hundred hospitals and rest houses. Under him the Khmer Empire reached its greatest extent.

lead.en: Georgia's golden age, from Caucasus power to Rustaveli's epic

summary.en: Tamar became sole ruler of Georgia, and her reign is remembered as the country's golden age. Georgia dominated the Caucasus, and Shota Rustaveli wrote The Knight in the Panther's Skin.

lead.en: A failed raid becomes the subject of a great epic

summary.en: In spring 1185, Prince Igor Svyatoslavich of Novgorod-Seversky attacked the Cumans, was defeated and captured. The campaign is the subject of The Tale of Igor's Campaign, the masterpiece of Old East Slavic literature.

lead.en: Saladin defeats the crusaders and takes Jerusalem

summary.en: Sultan Saladin destroyed the army of the Kingdom of Jerusalem at the Horns of Hattin and then took Jerusalem itself. Its loss provoked the Third Crusade, which failed to recover the city.

lead.en: Town self-government spreads east as far as Kyiv and Vilnius

summary.en: In 1188 Archbishop Wichmann confirmed the rights of Magdeburg’s citizens, and the town law that grew up there became the model for hundreds of towns in Central and Eastern Europe. A town under Magdeburg law elected its own council, judged its residents and ran its trade free of the local lord. Kraków, Vilnius, Minsk, Polotsk, Kyiv and Lviv received it; in the former Grand Duchy of Lithuania and in Ukraine it lasted into the first half of the 19th century.

lead.en: A village in a cliff alcove, the largest cliff dwelling in the US

summary.en: Tree-ring dates show Cliff Palace was built from about 1190 to 1260. The Ancestral Puebloans raised some 150 rooms and 23 round ritual chambers, or kivas, in an alcove beneath a cliff. By 1300 the people had left Mesa Verde, probably because of drought and conflict.

lead.en: Power shifts from court to samurai for nearly seven centuries

summary.en: Minamoto no Yoritomo, victor of the Genpei War, received the title of shogun and set up a military government at Kamakura. Real power passed from the imperial court to the samurai and stayed there for nearly seven centuries, until 1868.

lead.en: A Ghurid victory opens northern India to Muslim rule

summary.en: Muhammad of Ghor, beaten here the year before, returned with a new army and defeated the Rajput ruler Prithviraj Chauhan. The way into the Gangetic plain lay open: Delhi passed to the Ghurids, and their governor Qutb ud-Din Aibak founded the Delhi Sultanate in 1206.

lead.en: Ethiopia carves a 'New Jerusalem' out of solid rock

summary.en: Under the Ethiopian king Lalibela of the Zagwe dynasty, eleven monolithic churches were carved out of solid rock. Conceived as a 'New Jerusalem', the town remains a major pilgrimage site for Ethiopian Christians.

lead.en: At the edge of the world, the culture of the moai is born

summary.en: Polynesians settled Easter Island, one of the most remote inhabited islands on Earth; the date is debated. Its distinctive culture went on to carve nearly a thousand moai, giant stone statues of ancestors.

lead.en: Inuit ancestors crossed from Alaska to Greenland in two centuries

summary.en: Around the 12th–13th centuries, hunters of the Thule culture moved east from Alaska and in a short time spread across the whole Canadian Arctic to Greenland. They had dog sleds, large skin boats called umiaks and harpoons for whaling. The Thule displaced the earlier Dorset people and became the direct ancestors of today's Inuit.

lead.en: Inca legend: a city founded where a golden staff sank

summary.en: In Inca legend, the children of the Sun, Manco Cápac and Mama Ocllo, rose from Lake Titicaca and founded a city where their golden staff sank into the ground. Historians think the Incas built a small kingdom at Cusco around the start of the 13th century. For almost two centuries it was one of many in the Andes, until under Pachacuti it became an empire.

lead.en: A Tongan king's stone gateway, the 'Stonehenge of the Pacific'

summary.en: In the 13th century Tuʻitātui, the eleventh Tuʻi Tonga, raised a trilithon of coral limestone slabs, each weighing tens of tonnes, in the east of Tongatapu. The name means 'the Burden of Maui': legend says only the demigod could have carried such stones. It is known as the 'Stonehenge of the Pacific'.

lead.en: Hindu–Arabic numerals begin to replace Roman ones

summary.en: In 1202 Leonardo of Pisa, known as Fibonacci, published Liber Abaci, introducing Europeans to Hindu–Arabic numerals and positional notation. Merchants soon saw how much easier calculation became.

lead.en: Byzantium shatters and never regains its former strength

summary.en: Diverted by Venice, the Fourth Crusade stormed and sacked Christian Constantinople. Byzantium splintered into Latin and Greek states and never regained its former strength, while the rift between East and West deepened.

lead.en: The birth of history's largest land empire

summary.en: An assembly of Mongol nobles at the headwaters of the Onon proclaimed Temüjin Genghis Khan, supreme ruler of all the Mongols. Within decades the state he created became the largest contiguous land empire in history.

lead.en: Three centuries of Muslim rule over northern India begin

summary.en: After the death of Muhammad of Ghor, his general Qutb ud-Din Aibak became independent ruler of the conquered lands of northern India. The Delhi Sultanate dominated the north for over three centuries; the Qutb Minar became its emblem.

lead.en: A medieval engineer describes robots, pumps and an elephant clock

summary.en: Al-Jazari, engineer to the Artuqid court, wrote a book on some fifty devices, from water pumps to automaton musicians. The most famous is a water clock shaped like an elephant whose mechanical driver struck a drum every half hour.

lead.en: Cambridge University began as an escape from Oxford

summary.en: In 1209, after a clash between townsfolk and students, two Oxford scholars were hanged and a group of academics fled to Cambridge. Thus began the second-oldest university in the English-speaking world, Oxford's eternal rival.

lead.en: Thousands of youths set out to free Jerusalem unarmed

summary.en: In 1212 a youth named Nicholas led crowds of young people and paupers from Cologne towards the sea, promising it would part before them. It did not, and none reached the Holy Land; historians think chroniclers called the poor of any age "children".

lead.en: Barons curb the king — a root of the rule of law

summary.en: Under pressure from rebel barons, King John of England sealed Magna Carta. The charter curbed arbitrary royal power and became a cornerstone of the ideas of the rule of law and constitutional government.

lead.en: Genghis Khan captures the city that became Beijing

summary.en: Genghis Khan's Mongols besieged Zhongdu, capital of the Jurchen Jin empire, for more than a year and took it in 1215. The Jin court fled south to Kaifeng, and the city on the site of modern Beijing reportedly burned for over a month.

lead.en: The sons of Vsevolod the Big Nest clash in the bloodiest feud

summary.en: The dispute over Vsevolod the Big Nest's inheritance was settled near Yuryev-Polsky. Men of Novgorod, Smolensk and Rostov under Mstislav the Bold and Konstantin Vsevolodovich routed the armies of his brothers Yuri and Yaroslav. Konstantin won the throne of Vladimir; the chronicles count it among the bloodiest civil battles of Rus'.

lead.en: Revenge for slain merchants: Bukhara, Samarkand and Merv razed

summary.en: In 1218 the governor of Otrar massacred a Mongol trade caravan, and Shah Muhammad II of Khwarazm executed Genghis Khan's envoy. The Mongols invaded: in 1219–1221 Otrar, Bukhara, Samarkand, Urgench and Merv fell, and many of their people were slaughtered. The shah died a fugitive on an island in the Caspian.

lead.en: The last great Maya capital of Yucatán

summary.en: After Chichen Itza declined, the walled city of Mayapan, home to 15,000–17,000 people, became the leading city of northern Yucatán. The nobles of subject towns had to live in the capital, which was ruled by the Cocom family. In the mid-15th century it was destroyed in a revolt, and Yucatán broke into the small kingdoms the Spaniards found.

lead.en: Rus' first clash with the Mongols ends in a crushing defeat

summary.en: On 31 May 1223 the Mongol generals Jebe and Subutai crushed a combined army of Rus' princes and Cumans. It was the first clash between Rus' and the Mongols; many princes, including Mstislav of Kiev, were killed.

lead.en: An excommunicated emperor wins Jerusalem without a battle

summary.en: Emperor Frederick II set off on crusade while excommunicated by the Pope. Instead of fighting, he negotiated with Sultan al-Kamil of Egypt, and in 1229 a treaty returned Jerusalem to the Christians for ten years.

lead.en: The largest medieval manuscript, with a portrait of the Devil

summary.en: The giant manuscript weighs about 75 kg, and one page shows a full-length portrait of the Devil. Legend says a monk condemned to be walled up wrote it in a single night with the Devil's help; in reality it took decades.

lead.en: A medieval textbook on the round Earth, in use for 400 years

summary.en: Around 1230 the Paris master John of Sacrobosco wrote an astronomy textbook arguing that the Earth is a sphere. It was read in every European university for about 400 years and reprinted dozens of times after printing arrived.

lead.en: The Pope hands the hunt for heretics to special judges

summary.en: In 1231 Pope Gregory IX's bull Excommunicamus made the prosecution of heresy a matter for church courts, and from 1233 he appointed Dominican inquisitors, first of all against the Cathars of southern France. This was the start of the papal Inquisition.

title.en: Battle of Kirina and rise of Mali

lead.en: As the griots tell it, Sundiata's victory births an empire

summary.en: The Malinke leader Sundiata Keita defeated Sumanguru Kante, king of Sosso. The victory founded the Mali Empire, heir to West Africa's gold trade; Sundiata's story lives on in the epic of the griots.

lead.en: Russian principalities fall under the Golden Horde

summary.en: The army of Batu Khan sacked Ryazan, Vladimir and many other cities, and in 1240 Kiev. The Russian principalities fell under the overlordship of the Golden Horde for nearly two and a half centuries.

lead.en: Spain's last Muslim rulers build a palace-fortress

summary.en: Around 1238 Muhammad I, founder of the Nasrid dynasty, began a fortified residence on the hill above Granada. The Alhambra's carved halls and courtyards became the pinnacle of Moorish art.

lead.en: Thai chiefs throw off Khmer rule

summary.en: Around 1238 Thai chiefs expelled the Khmer governor from Sukhothai, and Si Inthrathit became its first king. Sukhothai is regarded as the first Thai state; under Ram Khamhaeng it spread Theravada Buddhism, and tradition credits him with the Thai script. In the 15th century the kingdom was absorbed by Ayutthaya.

lead.en: The Mongols destroy the ancient capital of Rus'

summary.en: In December 1240 Batu's army took Kiev after a siege. The last defenders sheltered in the Church of the Tithes, which collapsed. A few years later the papal envoy Carpini counted barely 200 houses in the city. The Mongols then moved on into Poland and Hungary.

lead.en: Victory over the Swedes earns Prince Alexander his epithet

summary.en: On 15 July 1240 Prince Alexander of Novgorod defeated a Swedish force where the Izhora joins the Neva. The victory later earned him the name Nevsky.

lead.en: A capital on the Volga; Rus' pays tribute for nearly 240 years

summary.en: Back from his European campaign, Batu founded the capital of Sarai on the lower Volga. His realm, later called the Golden Horde, ruled the steppe from the Danube to the Irtysh. Rus' princes received patents to rule from the Horde and paid tribute until the Great Stand on the Ugra in 1480.

lead.en: Alexander Nevsky halts the Livonian Order

summary.en: Forces led by Prince Alexander Nevsky defeated the knights of the Livonian Order on the frozen Lake Peipus. The victory checked the Order's eastward advance into the lands of Novgorod and Pskov and became an emblem of Russian military history.

lead.en: Nearly a thousand stone ancestors gaze inland

summary.en: By various estimates, between the 13th and 16th centuries the people of Rapa Nui carved nearly a thousand moai statues from volcanic tuff at the Rano Raraku quarry. They were set on stone ahu platforms with their backs to the sea, facing the villages their deified ancestors protected. The largest erected statue, Paro, is about 10 m tall; the unfinished "El Gigante" in the quarry is about 21 m.

lead.en: A mortarless stone city grows rich on gold

summary.en: On the plateau between the Zambezi and Limpopo rose the stone city of Great Zimbabwe, capital of a trading state of the ancestors of the Shona. Its walls were built without mortar, and its wealth came from gold traded through Swahili ports.

lead.en: A tiny gold figure that became a symbol of South Africa

summary.en: A rhino of thin gold foil over a wooden core was laid in a royal grave on Mapungubwe Hill in the 13th century. Found in the 1930s, it was long downplayed under apartheid; today South Africa's highest honour is named after its kingdom.

lead.en: 81,000 woodblocks carved as a prayer against the Mongols

summary.en: As the Mongols ravaged Goryeo, the court, sheltering on Ganghwa Island, commissioned a new edition of the Buddhist canon in hope of the Buddha's protection. Between 1237 and 1248 craftsmen carved more than 81,000 wooden printing blocks, almost without a single error. Kept at Haeinsa Temple since 1398, they are the most complete surviving Buddhist canon in Classical Chinese.

lead.en: A giant bronze Buddha has sat outdoors for 500 years

summary.en: Casting of the bronze Buddha, over 13 m tall with its base, began in 1252. Storms wrecked the hall around it several times, and in 1498 a tsunami washed it away; ever since, the Buddha has sat in the open air.

lead.en: The Grand Duchy of Lithuania is born

summary.en: Mindaugas united the Lithuanian lands, converted to Catholicism and received a royal crown from the pope, becoming Lithuania's only crowned king. His state, the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, would absorb most of western Rus', including Kiev, over the following centuries.

title.en: Daniel of Galicia crowned King of Rus'

lead.en: The prince of Galicia–Volhynia takes a royal crown from the pope

summary.en: Daniel Romanovych, ruler of Galicia–Volhynia, received a crown from Pope Innocent IV's legate at Drohiczyn, with the title King of Rus'. He hoped for Western help against the Mongols, but no crusade came, and Daniel had to submit to the Horde.

lead.en: Blast wipes out Pamatan and leaves traces at both poles

summary.en: In 1257 Samalas on Lombok exploded in one of the strongest eruptions in millennia, destroying the capital Pamatan. Its trace is found in ice at both poles; Europe's cold summer of 1258 and mass graves in London may be linked to it.

lead.en: The last caliph dies: a symbolic end to Islam's golden age

summary.en: The Mongol army of Hulagu stormed and sacked Baghdad, and the last Abbasid caliph, al-Musta'sim, was executed. The destruction of the caliphal capital and its libraries symbolically ended the Islamic Golden Age.

lead.en: The Mamluks deal the Mongols their first major field defeat

summary.en: The Mamluks of Egypt under Qutuz and Baybars defeated a Mongol army in Palestine. The first major Mongol defeat in open battle halted their advance in the Middle East and saved Egypt.

lead.en: After 57 years of Latin rule, the last dynasty begins

summary.en: A small force under the Nicaean general Alexios Strategopoulos entered Constantinople almost unopposed while the Latin garrison was away. Michael VIII Palaiologos restored the Byzantine Empire, and his dynasty ruled until the city fell in 1453.

lead.en: Islam takes root in Indonesia on Sumatra's northern coast

summary.en: In the later 13th century the port sultanate of Samudera Pasai arose on the northern coast of Sumatra. The gravestone of its first ruler, Malik al-Saleh, is dated 1297, the oldest evidence of a Muslim state in the archipelago. The name Samudera probably gave the whole island its name; Ibn Battuta visited in 1345.

title.en: Yekuno Amlak founds the Solomonic dynasty

lead.en: Kings claiming descent from Solomon rule until 1974

summary.en: In 1270 the prince Yekuno Amlak overthrew the Zagwe dynasty, builders of the Lalibela churches, and claimed the heritage of the ancient kings of Aksum. The new dynasty traced its line to a son of King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba, a legend set down in the epic Kebra Nagast. The Solomonids ruled Ethiopia for almost seven centuries, until Haile Selassie was deposed in 1974.

title.en: Kublai Khan founds the Yuan dynasty

lead.en: All of China falls under foreign rule for the first time

summary.en: Genghis Khan's grandson Kublai proclaimed the Yuan dynasty, with its capital at Khanbaliq (Dadu), on the site of modern Beijing. In 1279 the Mongols completed the conquest of the Song, bringing all of China under foreign rule for the first time.

lead.en: 17 years at Kublai's court open Asia to European eyes

summary.en: The Venetian Marco Polo travelled to China with his father and uncle and spent some 17 years at the court of Kublai Khan. His book of travels became Europe's chief source of knowledge about Asia for centuries.

title.en: Great Drought and the Pueblo exodus

lead.en: A long drought empties the cliff palaces of Mesa Verde

summary.en: Tree rings record a prolonged drought in the American Southwest from 1276 to 1299. By 1300 the Ancestral Puebloans had left the cliff dwellings of Mesa Verde and moved south, in the same years Marco Polo served at Kublai Khan's court.

lead.en: Humans reach the last large landmass left unsettled

summary.en: East Polynesian voyagers in canoes reached New Zealand, the last major landmass to be settled by humans. Their descendants created Māori culture; one of the oldest settlements has been found at Wairau Bar.

lead.en: Typhoons twice scatter Kublai Khan's fleets off Japan

summary.en: In 1274 and 1281 Kublai Khan's fleets sailed against Japan, and both times storms scattered them. The typhoon of 1281 sank much of a vast armada off Takashima; the Japanese called it kamikaze, the divine wind.

lead.en: Town records recall the day 130 children left Hamelin

summary.en: According to old records, on 26 June 1284 a piper led 130 children out of Hamelin. The rats only entered the story in the 16th century; what really happened is unknown, with theories ranging from disease to emigration east.

lead.en: Marco Polo in reverse: a monk from Beijing visits Paris

summary.en: Rabban Bar Sauma, a Nestorian monk from Khanbaliq (Beijing), reached Europe as envoy of the Mongol Ilkhan. In 1287 he met King Philip IV of France and King Edward I of England, then the Pope.

lead.en: Stakes hidden in a riverbed wreck Kublai Khan's fleet

summary.en: General Trần Hưng Đạo repeated a trick the Vietnamese had used against the Chinese back in 938: iron-tipped stakes were driven into the riverbed and hidden by the tide. The retreating Yuan fleet was lured into the estuary, and when the water fell the ships were impaled and destroyed or captured. So ended the third Mongol invasion of Đại Việt.

lead.en: The oldest surviving firearm

summary.en: This bronze barrel of about 3.5 kg was dug up in Manchuria in 1970 and is linked to a Yuan campaign of 1288. It is the oldest surviving firearm in the world; Europe would not see guns for several more decades.

lead.en: A Javanese empire sketches the outline of future Indonesia

summary.en: Raden Wijaya, exploiting a Mongol invasion of Java, founded Majapahit. Under the minister Gajah Mada its influence spread over most of present-day Indonesia, and it is seen as a forerunner of the Indonesian state.

title.en: Osman I founds the Ottoman state

lead.en: A small beylik seeds an empire that will last six centuries

summary.en: Around 1299 Osman I, leader of a Turkish beylik in Bithynia, became an independent ruler. The state he founded grew into the Ottoman Empire, which lasted more than six centuries.
